about: Side topic X6 (How do social scientists study energy and people?): six social-science methods matched to six questions a city might ask about a heat-pump programme, with what each can and cannot tell a modeller, the data it needs and its ethics. Prairie City and its council are fictional. Method-neutral: no method is ranked above another; each answers a different kind of question. The method summaries are this course's own, at awareness level; the reading ladder points to the codes of practice.

predict.q: Which question can the model answer by itself

options.label: How much the winter evening peak changes if 2,000 homes switch
Which programme design residents would choose

feedback.peak: Yes: given stated assumptions about the homes, an energy model computes the change in the peak.
feedback.why: No: reasons come from people, and interviews are one way to ask them.
feedback.pick: No: preferences come from people, and a choice experiment is one way to measure them.

methods.label: Survey
methods.def: set questions to a sample standing for many
methods.asks: How many, how much, how often, across a population.
methods.data: A questionnaire answered by a sample chosen to represent a population.
methods.gives: Shares and rates by household group, such as who has a heat pump or who struggles with bills.
methods.cannot: Why people act as they do, in depth; or whether a programme caused a change, without a comparison design.

methods.label: Interview
methods.def: open conversations with a few people
methods.asks: Why and how, in people's own words.
methods.data: Open conversations with a few chosen people, recorded and transcribed.
methods.gives: Reasons, barriers and assumptions worth testing, including ones a model leaves out.
methods.cannot: How common each view is across a city.

methods.label: Choice experiment
methods.data: Repeated choices between offers whose features vary, made by a sample of people.
methods.gives: How much each feature weighs, such as bill saving against control, for adoption scenarios.
methods.cannot: What people do once the offer is real: the choices are stated, not observed.

methods.label: Ethnography
methods.asks: How people live with energy, day to day.
methods.data: Long observation and conversation in homes or communities.
methods.gives: Routines a model's behaviour rules should reflect, such as how heating is really used.
methods.cannot: Numbers that hold for a whole city.

methods.label: Document-based policy analysis
methods.def: reading laws, rulings and case records
methods.asks: How rules came about, and who shaped them.
methods.data: Laws, rulings, official case records and the documents parties submitted, read and compared over time.
methods.gives: The rules and limits a model must respect, and which of them are open to change.
methods.cannot: Documents alone do not show how people experience the rules.

methods.label: Participatory mapping
methods.def: participatory: residents mark places on maps
methods.asks: Which places matter to people, and why.
methods.data: Residents mark places on maps, in workshops or online.
methods.gives: Map layers used to compare possible locations, to exclude or weigh, as in lesson A19.
methods.cannot: How the whole population feels, when few take part.

questions.text: What share of Prairie City's households had trouble paying an energy bill last year, by income group?
questions.why: Survey: one questionnaire to a sample chosen to represent all households gives shares by group.

questions.text: Why do landlords turn down a free efficiency upgrade for their rental homes?
questions.why: Interviews: open questions to a few landlords bring out reasons no one listed in advance.

questions.text: How much bill saving would a household trade for letting the utility adjust its thermostat at the peak?
questions.why: Choice experiment: people pick between offers that vary saving and control, revealing the trade-off they accept.

questions.text: How do families actually use their heating through a winter, and what does comfort mean to them?
questions.why: Ethnography: time spent with households shows routines people may not report in a survey.

questions.text: How did the state's rules for rooftop solar bill credits change over ten years, and who argued for what?
questions.why: Document-based policy analysis: statutes, rulings and submitted documents read and compared over the decade.

questions.text: Which places do residents want kept clear of a new solar farm, and why?
questions.why: Participatory mapping: residents mark the places that matter, which planners can turn into map layers.

peopleWhy.yes: People take part: ask the ethics board first what review and consent apply; an exemption or a waiver is its decision, under its process.
peopleWhy.partly: Mostly documents; once officials are interviewed, or identifiable personal records are used, ask the ethics board too.

selection.q: Does the survey difference show the programme's effect

options.label: Yes: the difference is the effect
Not by itself: the homes that joined may differ
No: surveys cannot measure energy use

feedback.yes: Not by itself: homes that joined may have used less before the programme (selection).
feedback.notalone: Right: joiners may differ before the programme; lesson M14's methods build a fair comparison.
feedback.no: No: a survey can record use or bills; the trouble is the comparison, not the survey.

facts.what: U.S. households reporting energy insecurity in 2020, about 34 million: difficulty paying energy bills, or a home kept at an unsafe temperature because of energy costs (EIA's Residential Energy Consumption Survey).
Households that answered the 2020 survey, by web or mail questionnaire, late 2020 to early 2021.

Method categories given codes of practice in a review of energy social science: experiments, literature reviews, data collection, data analysis, quantitative energy modeling, qualitative analysis and case studies.

stop.title: This side topic stops at choosing a method
stop.lede: Social-science methods enter the course as what each can tell a modeller and how to work with the people who use them; training in a method is beyond it.
